source.title: Understanding (Un)Reliability of Steering Vectors in Language Models
source.authors: Joschka Braun; Carsten Eickhoff; David Krueger; Seyed Ali Bahrainian; D. Krasheninnikov

record.tranche_reason: Applies difference-of-means activation steering in a broader set of behavior datasets and prompt formats, but does not test refusal itself or the refusal-specific versions in the claim.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates steering for 36 assistant-behavior datasets, not refusal/compliance to harmful user requests. Its steering-effect and geometry results are recorded as findings about the claim's subject, but they do not measure any listed version. The paper also cites the original refusal-direction study; cited results are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study measures CAA steering on 36 persona and assistant-behavior multiple-choice datasets in Llama2-7B chat. It never builds a harmful-minus-harmless direction, never ablates or adds a refusal direction, and never measures refusal rates. Arditi et al. is cited only as an example of a linear behavior direction. Its results concern steering-vector reliability in general, a related but different construct, so they go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that prompt type has measurable but limited influence on steering. They find that steering-vector performance depends on directional consistency of activation differences and on separability along the difference-of-means line, so steering is not universally effective.
record.recipe_differences: Uses CAA's mean difference of positive and negative activations, but adds the vector only at layer 13 and tests varied assistant behaviors rather than refusal. It does not ablate a refusal direction or assess general capability preservation.
record.method_sensitivity: Steering effect and anti-steerable fraction vary by dataset; prompt types produce vectors with pairwise cosine similarities from 0.07 to 0.86. The paper reports no prompt type consistently outperforming the others.

fits_no_version.finding: In Llama2-7B chat, CAA mean-difference steering at layer 13 shifts logits positively on average across 36 behavior datasets. About a third of samples move the opposite way, ranging from 3% to 50% by dataset. For the least steerable datasets the mean effect is negative for some prompt types (Figure 5). Datasets steer better when activation differences align with each other and positive and negative activations separate cleanly.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Difference-in-means steering works reliably only when the target behavior's per-example activation differences share a coherent direction; otherwise it is weak or counterproductive.

record.peer_reviewed: ICLR 2025 Workshop on Foundation Models in the Wild
record.problems: Only Llama2-7B chat and multiple-choice behavior datasets are tested. The study does not evaluate unrelated general capabilities, and it notes that prompt-type comparisons are sensitive to training-set size. Some reported steering outcomes are shown in figures rather than detailed numerical tables.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported dataset-level steering outcomes or individual activation-distribution plots are included; the paper presents many as figures, and the retained rows prioritize aggregate prompt-type results and the reported directional-agreement correlations.

untested.parts: No refusal direction, ablation, induced refusal, or capability check.
No transfer across languages or models.

record.verdict_notes: Relation changed from 'tests'/T3 to 'cites_only'/T6: refusal appears only as a cited example in the introduction. The paper's Figures 1 and 5 report different averages for the same 36-dataset, per-prompt-type setup; this may reflect different runs. The signs of the Spearman correlations in Figure 6 are garbled in the extracted text.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test a harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction, refusal ablation, induced refusal, or preservation of other abilities.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration evaluation.
No jailbreak suppression of the refusal direction or training against its ablation.
Does not compare refusal representations to affine, cone, or multiple-direction accounts.
Does not measure harmfulness judgments separately from refusal decisions.
No cross-language, model-variant, or base-to-instruct transfer test.
Does not vary refusal training or test how training determines refusal-direction structure.

rows.subject: Llama2-7B chat
rows.operation_detail: Added a CAA mean-difference steering vector at layer 13 during inference; trained on 250 samples and evaluated on 500 per dataset.
rows.measure: Mean steering effect on logit difference and anti-steerable sample fraction
rows.note: Aggregate across datasets; the paper says all prompt types have a net-positive mean shift, while about one-third of samples move in the opposite direction.
rows.check: Measures CAA steering on behavior datasets, not refusal, so it bears on no version. The 'partial' state has no version to refer to. Figure 5 reports different averages for the same condition (1.52 / 32.9% vs Figure 1's 1.30 / 33.2%); the paper is internally inconsistent.
